points.heading: One-word verb times
points.body:
Today we learn how Spanish shows WHEN an action happens. A verb is an action word (cantar = to sing). To conjugate means to change that word for who speaks and for the time of the action. When we tell facts as real, we are in the indicative mood: we are narrating, not wishing.

We start with simple tenses. «Simple» means the verb is ONE word. Think of five clocks: present (now/habit: canto), imperfect (ongoing or repeated past: cantaba), preterite (finished past: canté), future (later: cantaré), conditional (would: cantaría). The stem is what remains after dropping -ar/-er/-ir (cantar → cant-). The ending is the tip you add; changing it also changes the time.

Read the I-forms of cantar as one short story: canto (now) · cantaba (past, still open) · canté (past, closed) · cantaré (later) · cantaría (would).

Práctica: Write those five I-forms for cantar and for comer. Beside each one, note the «when» in your own words. Read them aloud in order.

Error común: Using cantaba when the event is fully finished. With a closed «yesterday», prefer canté.

points.heading: Two-word verb times
points.body:
Sometimes Spanish uses TWO words. That is a compound tense. Word one is a helper form of haber (he, has, ha…). Here haber does not mean «there is»; it is only a helper that changes with I/you/he. Word two is the participle: the «already done» form, usually ending in -ado or -ido (cantado, comido, vivido).

Build he cantado slowly: he is the helper, cantado is the participle. Together they mean the singing already happened and still matters now. The participle stays still while the helper walks: yo he cantado, tú has cantado, él ha cantado.

Práctica: Write he / había / habré / habría + cantado. Circle the helper and underline the participle. Say aloud: «two pieces: helper + already-done form».

Error común: Writing hemos comidos. The participle does not take plural -s here → hemos comido.

points.heading: One word or two?
points.body:
Now we learn to choose. Ask: am I pointing to a clear closed moment, or to something already done whose result is still alive?

Walk through three sentences with me. «Ayer terminé el libro» uses one word because yesterday closed. «Ya he terminado el libro» uses two words because the result still matters. «Leía cuando sonó el teléfono» sets a background (leía) and then a closed hit (sonó).

Práctica: Write three pairs with the same verb (one-word version and two-word version). Under each pair, explain your choice in half a line.

Error común: Forcing «Ayer he ido» when your home ear says «Ayer fui» for a closed yesterday.

lesson.summary: Learn to narrate WHEN an action happens: one-word forms and two-word forms (haber + already-done form), choosing with meaning.
